title: How he became 'Big Chief' and the 'Son of the Chief' joke
summary: He explains Indians in music are called 'Chief' and tells how Lanin's office called a substitute 'the son of the Chief'.

story.theme_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band monikers
story.community_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band names

blocks.x: What about 'Chief' and 'Big Chief,' when did they start calling you that? How long ago?
Well, most Indians that attain a certain amount of --

Fame, things like that, they always called them 'Chief.' They don't know your name but they know you're into -- 'Hey, Chief,' you know, that's how -- 'Big Chief,' that's how I was always known. In school out in California they used to call me 'Muscle Roar,' they just spelled my name around from Russell Moore to 'Muscle Roar.'
So in other words it was early in your

musical career that they started calling you "Big Chief." Let's see, you were -- in 1935 when you were in New Orleans they called you that.
I see, okay. Let's see now. You were with Jeter-Pillars and then there was Armstrong gave you the call -- around when was that? That was about when? 1944?

You know, I've got a cute story to tell you at the time I could not make the job with Lester Lanin. We'll cover Lester Lanin later. But it's fresh in memory, and one time I could not make the job and they had a little trombone player, small Italian dark sub-trombone player, in the band. So George Jaffe was a leader for the Lanin office at the affair at the Waldorf Astoria. So I'm pretty well known with all the people that come to them ballrooms. They ask about me, if they don't see me they ask Mr. Lanin or they ask George and I couldn't make it so this fellow is little Italian /take my place, I wasn't feeling well. So anyway, these people came by, "Where's Big Chief," and George got tired of saying that I couldn't make it, so he said, "We don't have Big Chief tonight but we have the son of the Chief," and the musicians all fell out (laughter), they had this little,
